verses.text: King Solomon ruled over all Israel.
These were his chief officials: Azariah son of Zadok was the priest.
Elihoreph and Ahijah, sons of Shisha, were royal secretaries. Jehoshaphat son of Ahilud kept the official records.
Benaiah son of Jehoiada was commander of the army. Zadok and Abiathar were priests.
Azariah son of Nathan was in charge of the district governors. Zabud son of Nathan was a priest and the king's close adviser.
Ahishar was in charge of the palace. Adoniram son of Abda was in charge of the forced labour.
Solomon had twelve district governors over all Israel. They provided food for the king and his household. Each one had to provide food for one month of the year.
These are their names: Ben-Hur, in the hill country of Ephraim.
Ben-Deker, in Makaz, Shaalbim, Beth Shemesh, and Elon Beth Hanan.
Ben-Hesed, in Arubboth. Sokoh and all the land of Hepher also belonged to him.
Ben-Abinadab, in all the hills of Dor. He was married to Taphath, Solomon's daughter.
Baana son of Ahilud, in Taanach and Megiddo, and all of Beth Shean next to Zarethan below Jezreel, from Beth Shean to Abel Meholah, and on past Jokmeam.

Ben-Geber, in Ramoth Gilead. The towns of Jair son of Manasseh in Gilead belonged to him, and so did the region of Argob in Bashan, with its sixty large cities with walls and bronze bars on the gates.
Ahinadab son of Iddo, in Mahanaim.
Ahimaaz, in Naphtali. He was married to Basemath, Solomon's daughter.
Baana son of Hushai, in Asher and in Bealoth.
Jehoshaphat son of Paruah, in Issachar.
Shimei son of Ela, in Benjamin.
Geber son of Uri, in Gilead, the land that had belonged to Sihon king of the Amorites and Og king of Bashan. He was the only governor over that whole region.
The people of Judah and Israel were as many as the grains of sand on the seashore. They ate and drank and were happy.
Solomon ruled over all the kingdoms from the Euphrates River to the land of the Philistines, as far as the border of Egypt. These countries paid him taxes and served him for his whole life.
Every day Solomon's household needed thirty measures of fine flour and sixty measures of ordinary flour,
ten fat cattle, twenty cattle from the pastures, and one hundred sheep, as well as deer, gazelles, roebucks, and fat poultry.
He ruled over all the kingdoms west of the Euphrates River, from Tiphsah to Gaza, and over all the kings west of the river. And he had peace on every side.
As long as Solomon lived, the people of Judah and Israel lived in safety, from Dan to Beersheba. Each family sat under its own grapevine and its own fig tree.
Solomon had forty thousand stalls for his chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen.
The district governors provided food for King Solomon and for everyone who ate at his table. Each one did this in his own month, and they made sure nothing was missing.
They also brought barley and straw for the chariot horses and the fast horses to the right places, each one doing his share.
God gave Solomon very great wisdom and understanding, and a mind as wide as the sand on the seashore.
Solomon's wisdom was greater than the wisdom of all the people of the east, and greater than all the wisdom of Egypt.
He was wiser than anyone else, even wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and wiser than Heman, Kalkol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol. He became famous in all the nations around.
He spoke three thousand proverbs, and he wrote one thousand and five songs.
He talked about plants, from the great cedar tree of Lebanon to the small hyssop plant that grows out of walls. He also taught about animals, birds, creatures that crawl on the ground, and fish.
People from every nation came to listen to Solomon's wisdom. They were sent by all the kings of the earth who had heard about his wisdom.
